title: Isomorphism criterion from a maximal torus and lifted simple root groups
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Reductive means smooth and connected with no nontrivial smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup; unipotent means that geometric points are unipotent matrices in a faithful representation. Split maximal tori, character lattices, roots, coroots, positive systems and simple-root bases are as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Let $H,G$ be reductive, let $S\subseteq H$ and $T\subseteq G$ be split maximal tori, and let $f:H\to G$ be a surjective homomorphism on underlying spaces such that $a=f|_S:S\xrightarrow{\sim}T$ is an isomorphism. Fix a simple-root base $\Delta$ for $(G,T)$ and root subgroups $U_\gamma$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations]. For every $\alpha\in\Delta$ and $\varepsilon\in\{1,-1\}$ assume there is a smooth connected closed subgroup $V_{\varepsilon\alpha}\subseteq H$, isomorphic to the additive group scheme $\mathbf G_a$ [def-sc-gm-ga], normalized by $S$, on which $S$ acts through $a^*(\varepsilon\alpha)$. Explicitly, for an isomorphism $v:\mathbf G_a\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{\varepsilon\alpha}$ one has $s v(x)s^{-1}=v((\varepsilon\alpha)(a(s))x)$ after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. Suppose that $f|_{V_{\varepsilon\alpha}}:V_{\varepsilon\alpha}\xrightarrow{\sim}U_{\varepsilon\alpha}$ is an isomorphism. Then $f$ is an isomorphism of group schemes. The case $\Delta=\varnothing$ is included. No reducedness or separability of the scheme-theoretic kernel is assumed.

source.place: Argument of 23.24 and the final paragraph completing 23.18, printed p.492, in the general form of a surjective reductive homomorphism with an isomorphism on maximal tori and lifted simple root groups; rank comparison and Weyl conjugation use 21.51 and 21.39, and the big cells use 21.84. This is a supporting criterion, not the isogeny existence theorem.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-affine-homomorphism-flat-image] to write $f=j q$ with $q:H\to I$ faithfully flat on coordinate algebras and $j:I\hookrightarrow G$ closed. Since $f$ is surjective on underlying spaces, so is $j$. The structural morphism of $G$ is smooth; [sbc-lem-smooth-geometrically-reduced] makes $G$ reduced. By [def-weil-closed-immersion], write $I=\operatorname{Spec}(F[G]/J)$. Every prime of $F[G]$ contains $J$, since $j$ is surjective. Thus $J$ lies in the nilradical, which is zero by [def-pc-reduced-scheme]. Hence $j$ is an isomorphism and $f$ is faithfully flat on coordinate algebras.

source.place: 23.24 and Theorem 5.39: scheme-theoretic image; smoothness supplies reducedness. The affine ideal argument is written out.

proof.text: Let $K=\ker f$, the closed subgroup defined by the fibre over the identity. For every $F$-algebra, $f(hkh^{-1})=f(h)1f(h)^{-1}=1$, so $K$ is normal. Its scheme-theoretic intersection with $S$ is $\ker a=1$, because $a:S\simeq T$. This is the identity scheme, not merely a statement about geometric points. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-normal-subgroup-torus-finiteness] to $H,S,K$. All its hypotheses hold and the intersection has coordinate algebra $F$, so $K$ has finite-dimensional coordinate algebra.

source.place: 23.24, p.492: reduce the kernel and use normal-subgroup rank comparison; supporting general criterion retains nonreduced kernels.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-isogeny-root-power-laws] to $f:H\to G$: step 1 gives faithful flatness, step 2 gives a finite scheme-theoretic kernel, and $f(S)=T$. Write $u=a^*:X^*(T)\xrightarrow{\sim}X^*(S)$. Obtain a bijection $b:\Phi_H\xrightarrow{\sim}\Phi_G$ and positive characteristic-exponent powers $e_\delta$ with $u(b\delta)=e_\delta\delta$ and $a_*(\delta^\vee)=e_\delta(b\delta)^\vee$. The same node says that $K$ is central exactly when all $e_\delta=1$. We will verify this condition without assuming separability.

source.place: Proposition 23.5(a),(b), pp.485--486; these results precede and do not use the isogeny existence theorem.

proof.text: For $\alpha\in\Delta$ and $\varepsilon=\pm1$, put $\lambda=u(\varepsilon\alpha)\ne0$. The closed immersion $V_{\varepsilon\alpha}\hookrightarrow H$ injects tangent spaces: on dual-number points this follows directly from injectivity of a closed immersion. Its one-dimensional tangent space has $S$-weight $\lambda$ by the assumed conjugation formula. Therefore $\lambda\in\Phi_H$; [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections] says that this weight space has dimension one. The uniqueness clause of [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] identifies $V_{\varepsilon\alpha}=U_\lambda$. The equation from step 3 gives $b\lambda=e_\lambda\varepsilon\alpha$, because $u$ is injective. Reducedness of $\Phi_G$ ([lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]) forces $e_\lambda=1$ and $b\lambda=\varepsilon\alpha$. In particular $u\alpha\in\Phi_H$ and $a_*((u\alpha)^\vee)=\alpha^\vee$ for each simple $\alpha$.

source.place: Final paragraph completing 23.18, p.492: identify the lifted simple root groups; Proposition 23.5 supplies the root and coroot relations.

proof.text: To apply root induction, use the rational root system of the target root datum. Its finite Weyl group and reflections are given by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. Apply [lem-sfb-root-datum-lattice-embedding] with $M=X^*(T)$ and the coroot functionals: all its reflection, finiteness and reducedness hypotheses hold. It supplies $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}\Phi_G$ and its restricted coroots spanning $E^\vee$. These spaces have the perfect evaluation pairing. The root datum gives simultaneous root/coroot reflection permutations and integer pairings. The simple-root base $\Delta$ is linearly independent, and each root or its negative is an integral nonnegative sum from it. Thus [lem-sfb-root-base-rational-integral-spans], applied to $E,E^\vee$, supplies the corresponding coroot independence and nonnegative expansion. This makes $\Delta$ a base of the rational root pairing in the precise sense required for reflection induction. Central torus directions have been removed, so no spanning hypothesis on $X^*(T)$ has been introduced.

source.place: Appendix C, root-system realization and bases, pp.612--615; supports Weyl propagation in the last paragraph of 23.18, p.492.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-root-base-reflection-induction] to the target rational root pairing of step 5 and the predicate $Q(\beta):\ u\beta\in\Phi_H$. Negation preserves $Q$ because the source root system is closed under negation. The simple roots satisfy $Q$ by step 4. If $Q(\beta)$ and $\alpha\in\Delta$, the source root reflection in $u\alpha$ sends $u\beta$ to $u\beta-\langle u\beta,(u\alpha)^\vee\rangle u\alpha$. The character/cocharacter pairing is natural under $a$, by composition of characters and cocharacters; using step 4 this expression equals $u(\beta-\langle\beta,\alpha^\vee\rangle\alpha)=u(s_\alpha\beta)$. Source reflections preserve roots by [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. These are exactly the three hypotheses of the cited induction node. Hence $u\beta\in\Phi_H$ for every $\beta\in\Phi_G$. For any $\delta\in\Phi_H$, step 3 now says that both $\delta$ and $u(b\delta)=e_\delta\delta$ are source roots. Source reducedness forces $e_\delta=1$.

source.place: Final paragraph completing 23.18, p.492: propagation from simple roots by Weyl reflections; Appendix C.22.

proof.text: By the centrality clause of [lem-sfb-isogeny-root-power-laws], step 6 implies that $K$ is central as a group scheme. Every element of $K(A)$ therefore commutes with all elements of $S(A\prime)$ after every $A$-algebra extension. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer] to $H,S$: the field is algebraically closed, $H$ is reductive and $S$ is maximal. Its scheme-theoretic equality $C_H(S)=S$ puts $K$ inside $S$ on every test algebra. Consequently $K=K\cap S=1$ by step 2. This rules out infinitesimal kernel factors as well as reduced ones.

source.place: Proposition 23.5(b), pp.485--486; Corollary 17.84, p.379; scheme-theoretic version of the conclusion after 23.24.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal] to $q=f$ and the identity homomorphism of $H$. It kills the trivial scheme-theoretic kernel, so there is $j:G\to H$ with $jf=\operatorname{id}_H$. Apply the uniqueness clause of that same node with $u=f:H\to G$: both $\operatorname{id}_G$ and $fj$ factor $f$ through itself, hence $fj=\operatorname{id}_G$. Therefore $f$ is an isomorphism. If $\Delta$ is empty, root induction in step 6 still applies (the induction node explicitly allows an empty base); all exponent assertions are vacuous when the root index set is empty, and the centrality, self-centralizer and quotient arguments are unchanged. In particular the torus-only and trivial-group cases are covered.

source.place: Conclusion of 23.18, p.492; faithfully flat quotient universal property (Theorem 5.21/5.28) gives the global inverse.

proof_origin.place: Argument of 23.24 and completion of 23.18, p.492, reorganized using the already existing Proposition 23.5 root-power/centrality node and reflection induction; no isogeny existence theorem is used.
